headline: A senator sued 81 of his patients. Now Kansas is close.
summary: Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in about a century. This year Sen. Roger Marshall is close enough to losing that Trump flew to Wichita on Monday to rally for him. Marshall, once a doctor, sued 81 former patients over unpaid bills, and some went to jail. Diesel and fertilizer prices are up. He debates Adam Hamilton Wednesday.

cover_question.q: Can a doctor sue his patients?

cover_answer: Yes, and he did, 81 times. Now voters weigh in.
table_question: Is it fair to chase money you're owed if the person can't pay?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Kansas, people are choosing who will speak for them in Washington, and the man who has the job might lose it. He used to be a doctor, and he took 81 of his patients to court because they hadn't paid him. For years his team won Kansas easily, like a runner with a huge head start, but this time the other runner is right behind. The grown-ups vote in two weeks, and that settles it.
5-7.why: A head start, and the other runner closing. The rest can wait.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands them the one that holds: a doctor took 81 of his own patients to court. The head start is the picture of a safe seat; the runner closing is why anyone is talking about Kansas. Expect "did the sick people get in trouble?" Some did, for ignoring the court.

8-12.script: Senator Roger Marshall used to deliver babies in Great Bend, Kansas. When 81 patients didn't pay, he sued them, and some went to jail for ignoring the court. He also walked out of a town hall, and both became ads against him. An election is the referee's whistle, and Kansas blows it in two weeks.
8-12.why: Bills, lawsuits, walkout, close race. One chain.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether adults are held to the rules they hold others to. The script gives them the chain in order: unpaid bills, lawsuits, a walkout, ads, a close race. The referee is the voter. Expect "was he allowed to sue them?" Yes. Kansas is asking whether a doctor should, and that one has no rulebook.

13-17.script: A senator sued 81 former patients over medical bills, and some went to jail for ignoring the court. Was he collecting what he was owed, or punishing people who couldn't pay? Trump says the law required it. Diesel and fertilizer prices are up on Kansas farms. Which moves voters more, the lawsuits or the prices?
13-17.why: Owed or punished, then lawsuits or prices.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the debts were real, and the people jailed over them were low-income single mothers. The script asks them to weigh that pair, then a second one, the lawsuits against the fuel prices. Expect "would you vote for him?" Answer honestly, with reasons; they are testing whether you argue straight.

5-7.q: Why did the doctor take people to court?
5-7.a: They owed him money for their care. A court can make people pay, and some who ignored it went to jail.

8-12.q: Can a doctor sue his patients?
8-12.a: Yes. He sued 81 who hadn't paid. Trump says the law made him.

8-12.q: Why is Kansas close this time?
8-12.a: The lawsuits, the walkout, and fuel prices on the farms.

13-17.q: Was he owed, or was he punishing them?
13-17.a: Both can be true. Some who were jailed were single mothers.

13-17.q: Does a close race change a senator?
13-17.a: He promised lower fuel prices Monday, with no plan. Watch the debate.
